title: Quantitative Trading
answer: Market microstructure, factor models, execution learning, statistical arbitrage and regime shifts.

children.name: High-Frequency Market Microstructure
children.blurb: High-frequency market microstructure is the study of how orders, quotes, and trades interact at subsecond and millisecond timescales, including order book dynamics, bid-ask spreads, latency, and price impact.

children.name: Non-Linear Factor Models
children.blurb: Non-linear factor models describe asset returns as a function of predictors where the relationship can include interactions, thresholds, and regime-dependent effects that linear factor models miss.

children.name: Learning Trade Execution
children.blurb: Learning trade execution refers to the use of machine learning to decide how, when, and where to place orders in financial markets, rather than what to trade.

children.name: Statistical Arbitrage
children.blurb: Statistical arbitrage is a set of quantitative trading strategies that seek to profit from temporary mispricings between related financial instruments, using statistical models rather than economic fundamentals.

children.name: Detecting Market Regime Shifts
children.blurb: Detecting market regime shifts means identifying when the statistical behavior of a market changes, such as moving from low volatility to high volatility or from trending to mean reverting.

sections.body: Quantitative trading uses mathematical models and computation to decide what to buy or sell, when, and at what price. Artificial intelligence is now doing concrete work in this field, not just theoretical research. Machine learning models read order book updates and trade prints to predict short term price moves in high frequency market microstructure. Non linear factor models replace older linear regressions to find combinations of company and market data that explain returns. Reinforcement learning systems are trained to break large orders into smaller child orders to reduce market impact. Statistical arbitrage programs scan hundreds of securities for temporary price relationships that have drifted apart. Regime detection models use clustering and hidden state models to flag when the market's behavior has changed from calm to stressed.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is real but uneven. High frequency microstructure prediction is well developed for very short horizons, but profits are small per trade and depend on low latency infrastructure. Non linear factor models can find patterns that linear models miss, yet they are prone to overfitting and often fail out of sample. Learning trade execution has moved from research into production at some trading desks, but it is hard to prove that a learned policy beats a simple schedule like volume weighted average price in all market conditions. Statistical arbitrage works until crowded trades unwind, and its edge has narrowed as more firms use similar data. Detecting regime shifts is useful for risk management, but the shift is usually clear only after it has happened, so the honest limit is that these models are descriptive more than predictive.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to understand the raw mechanics of short term price formation should start with High-Frequency Market Microstructure, which explains order flow, spreads and latency. Non-Linear Factor Models then shows how machine learning builds on that microstructure data and broader fundamentals to forecast returns. Learning Trade Execution connects those forecasts to the practical problem of getting orders filled without moving the price against you. Statistical Arbitrage takes a portfolio view, looking for relative mispricings across many assets rather than a single price path. Detecting Market Regime Shifts sits across all of these, because a model that works in one market state often breaks in another, and this page describes how to recognize when the ground has changed.
